SETUP NOTE: the environment had zero public books, so the positive path was constructed by PATCHing the CP-5 throwaway to public through the real /v1/sharing route with a minted dev JWT, and REVERTED to private afterwards -- confirmed by the catalogue returning total=0 again. No book was left published.

composition_arc_apply.note: PROVEN end to end -- SUCCESS path reached (arc_id + chapter_ids + scene_ids returned) -- and it uncovered a two-layer defect that made 5 books permanently unopenable. FIRST INVOCATION took four preconditions the tool never names: an x-session-id header, a Work, an arc template, and MOTIFS in the book matching the template placements' motif_code (placements carry motif_id:null and resolve by CODE). Built them: created duel/ambush/meet as book_shared motifs with beats via composition_motif_create. Error taxonomy up to that point is genuinely good -- NO_MATERIALIZABLE_PLACEMENTS 'no placement resolved to a motif with beats', NO_CHAPTERS 'materialize maps onto existing chapters -- create chapters first', typed codes with actionable details. LAYER 1, the false message: a Work awaiting its knowledge-project backfill answered {'code':'BAD_REFERENCE','detail':'project None has no composition_work row'} -- false twice over, since the composition_work row EXISTS and it is the PROJECT that is absent, with a Python None leaked into a caller-facing string and no satisfier. Cause: _book_or_deny is the documented canonicalization point (D-COMPOSITION-ID-TRAP) and its docstring orders every caller to re-bind pid from meta.project_id; ten sites do, and none considered that value being NULL for a Work created while knowledge-service was down (C16/WG-3). Added _require_project(meta), applied at all ten, with a guard that counts them -- 10 gated, exactly 1 bare read (inside the helper), so a bypass reds. DATA: 82 of 516 Works (15.9%) NULL project_id, all 82 flagged pending. A/B confirmed the discriminator: the same tool and template against a BACKED Work answers a clean NO_CHAPTERS. LAYER 2, found by checking my own satisfier before shipping it -- the message names composition_create_work, and that tool answered 'not found or not accessible' for the very book it was supposed to heal. Not universal: it healed two other pending books (pending count 82 -> 80). The discriminator is whether the book's knowledge project ALREADY exists. The pending-row backfill lives only on _resolve_or_create_default_project's project-CREATE branch, so a book resolving to an EXISTING project skipped it; then works.get(pid) cannot see the pending row (it keys on project_id, which is NULL), works.create collides with the one-Work-per-book constraint, and the re-get by project_id misses for the same reason -- landing on a `raise uniform_not_accessible` whose own comment calls it defensive and unreachable. It was reachable for 5 of 80 pending Works, permanently, on every retry. Fixed by adopting the pending row before creating: get_pending_for_book -> backfill_project -> return it. LIVE: the throwaway's pending Work was adopted keeping its own id (019fea46-87a7...) bound to the pre-existing project 019fed4a..., pending=false, no duplicate row -- and composition_arc_apply then SUCCEEDED through it. TESTS: 4 guards (helper behaviour with a bound-project control, refusal wording, the 10-site wiring count, and the adopt-before-create ORDERING -- ordering is the whole fix, since adopting after the create is the collision it avoids). Both falsified RED. Full composition unit suite 3593 passed; one pre-existing test went red first and was a genuine catch -- its bare AsyncMock auto-created get_pending_for_book as truthy and swallowed the create it asserts, so the greenfield stub now states the absence explicitly. DEBRIS: three motifs and one applied arc left in the CP-5 throwaway book, by design.

composition_arc_assign_chapters.note: PROVEN by constructing its first invocation against the real arc #142 created (019ff01c-45c6...), and it was reporting DOING NOTHING as success. Five calls: assigning two chapter nodes worked (assigned:2), unassigning with structure_node_id:null worked (assigned:1) -- and then an unknown chapter_node_id, an unknown structure_node_id, and an EMPTY list all returned {'assigned': 0} with no error and no way to tell them apart. Three different mistakes, one success-shaped answer. A caller that mistypes one of the two uuids it must supply is told the write went through having changed nothing, and the repeated-failure breaker never fires either, because nothing failed. The repository is RIGHT to no-op -- its EXISTS guard is what stops an arc adopting another book's chapters, and the docstring says so. The handler simply returned the count without reading it. Fixed there: when the caller named chapters and none were assigned, diagnose which of the two preconditions failed -- the structure node is looked up and its book_id compared, so 'not an arc in this book' and 'none of those are active CHAPTER-kind outline nodes in this book' are separate messages with separate satisfiers (composition_arc_list, composition_list_outline). The second also names the id-confusion the tool invites: these are OUTLINE NODE ids, not book chapter ids. The EMPTY list deliberately stays a success -- asking to move no chapters is satisfied by moving none, and erroring there would break the idempotent 'ensure unassigned' shape and hand the model a failure it cannot act on. The guard is `count == 0 and args.chapter_node_ids`, and a test asserts the unconditional `count == 0` form is absent. composition_arc_edit(op=assign_chapters) DELEGATES to this handler, so one fix covers both surfaces. LIVE on the deployed image (container == built 683e6ee05136): both wrong-id cases now name their own cause, the empty list still returns assigned:0 as success, and a real assign still returns assigned:1. Falsified RED by deleting the diagnosis. Full composition unit suite 3596 passed.

composition_arc_delete.note: PROVEN by a full delete/restore round trip on the real arc from #142, which had two member chapters assigned in #143. The mechanics are sound: delete returns archived:true with an undo_hint naming composition_arc_restore and the exact node_id; restore returns archived:false with the inverse hint; re-deleting an already-archived arc is idempotent (the same shape as book_structure_part_archive in #138, and correct for the same reason -- the state asked for is the state that holds); an unknown node_id gives the uniform deny, which is right HERE because node_id is the only scope argument, so an unresolvable node means no grant was ever proven. THE DEFECT WAS THE DESCRIPTION, and it was a false statement of mechanism rather than a style problem. It read 'Member chapters are NOT deleted -- their structure_node_id simply points at an archived node.' Measured across the round trip: before delete 2 chapters carry structure_node_id=<arc> and 0 carry archived_from=<arc>; after delete it is 0 and 2; after restore it is 2 again. Membership is CLEARED into the recovery slot (archived_from_structure_node_id) and moved back on restore -- the opposite of the claim. This matters concretely: a caller who believed it would query the outline by structure_node_id after archiving, find nothing, and conclude the chapters were lost, which is precisely the fear the sentence existed to calm. The corrected text keeps the true reassurance (NOT deleted), states that they DO leave the arc into a recovery slot, and names what brings them back. Verified on the DEPLOYED image by reading the live tools/list, not the source. NOTE for whoever consumes this through the gateway: ai-gateway caches the federated tool list, so a description change needs a gateway restart to re-federate.

composition_arc_edit.note: PROVEN across all six ops with no code change needed -- the best-built tool the loop has measured, and the one that VERIFIES #143's fix reached both surfaces. The risk in a flat-superset op tool is that only `op` is required at the schema, so every per-op companion argument is a runtime check that can degrade into a generic refusal. All seven missing-argument paths name the op AND the argument: 'op=create requires book_id', 'op=update requires node_id and expected_version', 'op=assign_chapters requires book_id and chapter_node_ids', and so on. Nothing generic, nothing that leaves the caller guessing which of eighteen optional fields the op wanted. DELEGATION PARITY PROVEN, not assumed: the source comment claims arc_edit delegates to the legacy handlers with 'NO logic moved'. op=assign_chapters with a bad chapter id returned #143's new diagnosis verbatim through the unified surface, so one fix genuinely covered both entry points. Optimistic concurrency is exemplary: op=update with expected_version=999 returned {'success': false, 'outcome': 'applied_conflict', 'error': 'stale expected_version -- refetch and retry', 'current_version': 1} -- it hands back the value needed to retry rather than making the caller go and read it. op=update with the correct version, op=move under a parent and back to root (new_parent_arc_id=null), op=delete and op=restore all behaved. RECORDED, not fixed: undo hints minted through this tool name the LEGACY tools (composition_arc_restore / composition_arc_delete), which are visibility:legacy and hidden from the default discovery surface -- so a model that used the unified tool is handed an undo pointing at a tool it cannot see. That is the direct consequence of the 'preserved verbatim' delegation the comment promises. It stays recorded rather than fixed because #122 established that undo_hint is explicitly non-contractual and has no consumer in the tree; if one ever appears, this is the first thing it will trip over. Debris: the arc created for this iteration was deleted at the end.

composition_arc_extract_template.note: PROVEN, and it exposed a BA5 mechanism that had NEVER run in production. Extract itself works -- from the arc #142 applied it returned template_id, 2 member chapter nodes, 2 layout placements, 2 pacing chapters. But the extracted template's placements carried motif_code == motif_id == '019ff005-9674-...', where the real codes were 'duel' and 'meet'. A library arc template exists to be applied to ANOTHER book; a placement naming a uuid resolves there to nothing. Every extracted template was silently unportable while looking perfectly well-formed. ROOT CAUSE, and it is not in this tool. arc_apply.py has TWO apply functions. arc_apply() sets both the first-class structure_node_id (its comment: arc conformance reads WHERE structure_node_id = $arc) and annotations.motif_code (its comment: 'lets extract rebuild layout without re-resolving motifs'). Nothing in app/ calls it. Production -- the MCP tool AND the REST materialize route -- runs apply_arc_to_spec(), which built its ledger rows as {**row, 'outline_node_id': ...} and wrote NEITHER field. The only caller of the other function is tests/integration/db/test_arc_apply_roundtrip.py, so the suite stayed green over a mechanism with a 100% miss rate. DATA: 0 of 47 motif_application rows carried structure_node_id, 0 carried motif_code -- including the four rows a successful apply had just written. Two consequences: arc conformance's arc-scoped query matched nothing, and the round trip was lossy in exactly the field that makes a template reusable. FIXED at both ends. The write: apply_arc_to_spec now pins arc_id_str and looks the code up from the already-resolved motifs. The read: the extract fallback no longer disguises the uuid as a code -- rows written before the fix still have none, so the fallback must stay, but it now emits an EMPTY code while using the id only as a GROUPING key (an empty key would merge two motifs sharing a thread). motif_id is preserved either way and apply prefers a pinned id, so a legacy placement still resolves inside its owner's library. LIVE on the deployed image: a fresh apply took the ledger from 0/47 to 4 rows carrying structure_node_id and the codes 'duel'/'meet'; extracting from that arc produced placements with motif_code='duel'/'meet' and the ids intact -- the apply/extract round trip closing correctly for the first time. Full unit suite 3601 passed. RECORDED as DQ-18, not guessed: the template's tracks/roster (2 and 2) do not survive onto the arc node, so the extracted template has tracks:0 while its placements still name threads 'combat'/'romance'. The extractor faithfully copies what the node holds; the loss is upstream in apply, and which behaviour is intended is a product decision the code does not settle.

composition_arc_get.note: PROVEN by constructing its first invocation, and the READ was fine -- it was what the read revealed that mattered. The tool returns the node plus `version` (the OCC token composition_arc_edit needs, so the two compose without a second call), the cascade-resolved tracks/roster/roster_bindings, the derived span, and the open_promises rollup; an unknown node_id gives the uniform deny, correct here because node_id is the only scope argument. THE FINDING: it reported arc_template_id:null for an arc composition_arc_apply had just materialized FROM template 019f0d28. composition_arc_template_drift exists to answer 'did this arc drift from the TEMPLATE it came from (its pinned arc_template_id + template_version)?' -- so with the provenance unwritten it had nothing to answer about. DATA: 1 of 137 arc/saga nodes carried an arc_template_id, and apply is the only thing that creates an arc from a template. Unlike DQ-18's tracks/roster question this is NOT a design choice, which is why it got fixed while that got recorded: the column exists, composition_arc_edit(op=create) accepts it as a first-class argument, the drift tool names it as its input, and StructureRepo.update already whitelists it. It was simply never written on the one path holding the value. apply_arc_to_spec now stamps both halves after the commit that mints the arc -- best-effort and outside the commit transaction on purpose, because the outline tree is already correct by then and failing a real apply over a metadata label trades something real for something descriptive; the failure logs rather than passing silently. LIVE on the deployed image (c7b1f0ba83d5): a fresh apply then composition_arc_get returned arc_template_id 019f0d28... and template_version 1, and the population moved 1/137 to 2/138 -- every apply from here stamps it. Full unit suite 3604 passed.

composition_arc_import_analyze.note: PROVEN on the PROPOSE half without spending tokens -- it is tier W and async, so the first invocation returns a signed confirm_token carrying descriptor 'composition.arc_import', a title and a $2.00 estimate, and nothing runs until confirmed. An unknown import_source_id gives the uniform deny, correct here because import_source has no visibility column and is structurally un-shareable, so there is a real oracle to deny. THE FINDING was the third argument path: a malformed uuid answered 'badly formed hexadecimal UUID string' -- Python's own message, naming no argument. Measured across seven composition tools, IDENTICAL every time, and composition_arc_edit alone accepts seven uuid fields, so the caller was told one of them was wrong without being told which. TRAFFIC: 1 occurrence in 1448 tool-call messages -- thin, and it is the CONTENT of that one that justified acting. composition_arc_suggest received '...cb-1bc5-7384-9fb4-9fb4-3435368886d0': a model that DUPLICATED a uuid segment. Handed its own string back it can see that; told the string is badly formed it cannot. Echoing the value supplies information the caller has no other way to obtain, which is what separates this from the rewording the runbook rules out. Fixed as a 204-site sweep behind a _uuid(value, field) helper. THE FIRST PASS WAS WRONG AND THE LIVE A/B CAUGHT IT: I rewrote only `UUID(args.x)` (105 sites), and arc_edit and arc_suggest still leaked, because tools taking plain parameters parse `UUID(book_id)` instead -- 99 more. A guard asserting only the first shape was zero would have called that sweep complete, so the test now checks BOTH shapes. Deliberately NOT swept: 23 sites parsing server-supplied ids (an owner_user_id read from the database, a book_id decoded from a confirm token this service itself signed, tc.user_id from the envelope, comprehension variables). A malformed one there is a server fault with no caller argument to name, and dressing it as 'book_id must be a UUID' would send the caller hunting for a mistake it did not make. A test pins that exclusion so the next sweep does not 'finish the job'. LIVE on the deployed image (5cac8fdd1cc7): all seven tools name their field and echo the value, the corpus's duplicated group is visible in the message, and both controls (the real propose, a real arc read) are unregressed. Full unit suite 3609 passed.

composition_arc_list.note: PROVEN by constructing its first invocation; no code change needed, and the interesting part is a defect I nearly reported against it. include_archived=true returned 4 nodes while the book had 6 structure_node rows, which looks exactly like a listing dropping data. It is not: the other two are kind='part' -- the manuscript parts created in #139 -- and this tool lists the saga/arc axis, as its description says. PARTS AND ARCS SHARE THE structure_node TABLE, which is what makes a naive count the wrong denominator; against the right one (kind IN ('saga','arc')) the listing is 4 of 4. Checking the control before writing the finding is the only reason this is not a false report. Everything else holds. Default excludes archived (1 of 4); include_archived=true returns all four; ordering is depth then rank and the returned sequence '9','i','i','i' is correctly sorted (ASCII '9' < 'i'); an unknown book gives the uniform deny; and omitting book_id outside a studio answers 'book_id is required' rather than guessing -- the same ambient_book shape book_structure_read has (#139). It also shows #147's fix from the read side: the listed arc carries arc_template_id 019f0d28..., so a caller can now see which arcs came from a template without a per-node fetch, which is precisely the N+1 this tool exists to avoid. OBSERVED, not a defect: three of the four arcs are titled 'W10 FE Smoke Arc' and are distinguishable only by id -- debris from this loop's own repeated applies, not a product problem.

composition_arc_move.note: PROVEN, and it is the most serious defect of the phase: a legal-looking move SILENTLY produced a subtree past the depth cap the tool advertises. The description promises four rejections -- saga given a parent, nesting past saga→arc→sub-arc, a cycle, a cross-book parent -- and all four do refuse. It also promises to 'recompute the whole moved subtree's depth', and that is where it broke. The recompute was ONE recursive UPDATE touching every descendant at once, relying on the BEFORE trigger to derive each row's depth from its parent. Within a single statement the trigger fires per row in an UNSPECIFIED order, so a grandchild could be processed before its parent's new depth was written and derive its own from the stale value. Measured: after moving arc C from root to depth 1, its grandchild B recorded depth 2 while B's parent A was also 2 -- B was genuinely at depth 3, past the cap, and the trigger never objected because the depth it validated was the wrong one. DATA: 1 of 8 parented structure_node rows inconsistent (depth <> parent.depth+1), and it was the row that move had just created. A silent cap breach is worse than the refusal it replaced, because the column still reads as valid to everything downstream. Fixed with one statement per level, so each completes and its triggers run before the next begins; bounded by _MAX_SUBTREE_LEVELS=10 rather than the current cap of 2, since hardcoding the cap would reintroduce the same class on the next cap change. LIVE: moving C back to root repaired A and B and took the whole-table invariant to 0; then the exact move that had corrupted them was REFUSED and rolled back, with the tree unchanged. SECOND DEFECT, misattributed blame: a cycle was reported as a depth violation. The trigger checks depth before it walks for a cycle, and with the cap at 2 a node moved under its own descendant almost always trips depth first -- so the caller was told to find a shallower parent when the real problem was that the target sits BENEATH it. Advice that cannot succeed is worse than none; a model follows it in circles. Added a bounded ancestor walk BEFORE the repo call that names the relationship and points at composition_arc_list. The trigger stays the integrity SSOT -- this only names the cause its ordering hides. METHOD NOTE worth as much as the fixes: I first labelled a cycle case as 'depth' because all four test ids shared the prefix 019ff06f and I read ancestry off truncated ids. Re-reading the tree BY TITLE is what turned an apparent regression into the real finding. Full unit suite 3617 passed; the iteration's arcs were archived afterwards.

composition_arc_restore.note: PROVEN with no code change, and it is the correct answer to a trap this repo has been caught by before: a SYMMETRIC un-archive orphans a node. Restore here is deliberately asymmetric and both halves were measured. DOWNWARD: archiving C cascaded to its subtree (A and B archived); restoring C brought the whole subtree back. UPWARD: with all four archived, restoring the DEEPEST node alone (B) also un-archived its ancestor chain A and C, so B came back reachable from a visible root instead of stranded under archived parents. SCOPED: the unrelated saga stayed archived through every one of those operations -- the reconnect follows the chain, it is not a blanket un-archive of the book. Restoring an already-active node is idempotent (archived:false, same shape as book_structure_part_archive in #138 and arc_delete in #144). An unknown node_id gives the uniform deny, correct here because node_id is the only scope argument. The undo_hint names composition_arc_delete with the same node_id. Together with #144 this closes the delete/restore pair: member chapters move into the recovery slot and back, the subtree follows its root in both directions, and the ancestor chain is repaired on the way up.

composition_arc_template_archive.note: PROVEN with no code change: it does exactly what its description says, and the write is SAFE -- the UPDATE is scoped WHERE (owner_user_id = $1 OR (book_shared AND book_id = $3)) AND id = $2, so a foreign row is genuinely untouched rather than silently modified. That was the half worth verifying in code, because a tool that answers 'archived: true' for someone else's row is one line away from having archived it. THE FINDING is recorded as DQ-19 rather than fixed. The description justifies its no-op-success as an anti-oracle: 'a foreign/missing/system row is a uniform no-op (returns archived:true -- no existence oracle)'. Its documented inverse then gives the oracle back. Measured: archive(nonexistent) -> archived:true, restore(nonexistent) -> uniform deny; archive(mine) -> archived:true, restore(mine) -> the full row. Archive-then-restore distinguishes existence perfectly. The leak is narrow, since restore requires ownership, so what it reveals is 'this is MY archived template' versus not -- the caller's own data. The cost is borne by the honest caller: a typo'd id reports success. That is the same shape #143 fixed on arc_assign_chapters, with one decisive difference -- there the silent zero was undocumented, here it is a stated deliberate choice, and the loop does not reverse a documented security posture on its own authority.

composition_arc_template_create.note: PROVEN with no code change. Five calls: a minimal create returns the private template; a duplicate code is refused with 'an arc template with this code already exists'; visibility=public and visibility=unlisted are both refused with 'create makes a PRIVATE template; publish or share it from the studio UI'; and a create carrying typed threads + a layout placement + chapter_span persists them. Threads/layout/roster are $ref'd typed schemas rather than free-form objects, so a malformed placement is a schema rejection rather than a row of junk. CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the refusal points an AGENT at a UI, which is normally the 'affordance gate with no path to satisfy it' failure. Here it is correct -- there is no agent-callable publish for arc templates (composition_publish is about canonizing a CHAPTER), and the description says publishing is a deliberate human action behind a quota gate. The message honestly hands off to the human instead of naming a tool that does not exist, which is the right shape for an intentionally human-gated action. OBSERVED, not filed as a defect: the visibility enum advertises private|unlisted|public while two of the three always fail. Narrowing it to ['private'] would make the mistake impossible at the schema, but it would also replace a message that explains WHY and where to go with a bare enum-validation error. The current design trades a stricter schema for a more useful refusal, and having read the refusal, that trade is defensible.

composition_arc_template_drift.note: PROVEN with no code change, and it is the CONSUMER that #147 brought back to life. Against the arc that iteration stamped, drift returns available:true with a real report -- scope, chapter_count, thread_progress per thread, pacing, succession, unmaterialized placements. Before #147 that same arc had no arc_template_id, so this tool's answer would have been available:false: the fix and this iteration are the two halves of one finding. The 'unknown' branch its description promises is honest and specific: an arc authored directly returns {available:false, reason:'arc has no template provenance (authored directly)'} -- it names the state and why, rather than an empty report the caller might read as 'no drift'. That distinction matters here more than usual, since zero drift and no provenance would otherwise look identical. project_id is required alongside node_id and omitting it produces the kit's validation directive naming the field. Its description explains WHY the second id exists -- the Work's book must be the arc's book, so the pair cannot be used as a cross-book oracle. CHECKED, not a defect: the report's `arc_id` came back equal to the arc_template_id rather than the structure_node the caller passed. The code comments it as deliberate -- `arc_id` is the AXIS identity, which is structure_node.id on the spec path and arc_template.id on the template-drift path, with arc_template_id carrying provenance. Worth knowing that the report never echoes the node you asked about, but it is documented and consistent, not the field mislabel it resembles (contrast #146, where motif_code genuinely held a uuid).

composition_arc_template_edit.note: PROVEN, and op=update had NEVER worked -- on this tool OR its legacy twin. Every update failed with `null value in column "visibility" of relation "arc_template" violates not-null constraint`, and the field the caller asked to change was not written. It failed with one field supplied, with ALL fields supplied, and through composition_arc_template_update as well, against the tool's own promise that 'only the fields you pass change'. The repo was innocent: ArcTemplateRepo.patch builds its SET list from model_dump(exclude_unset=True), so an unmentioned field is meant to stay untouched. The MCP handler rebuilt the patch model from a PLAIN model_dump(), which materialises every optional field as an explicit None -- so the repo saw them all as set and emitted visibility = NULL. The irony is one line up: the unified tool already drops unset fields with _present(), whose own docstring says a flat-superset op tool 'must never force None onto a field whose default is a non-None value'. That care was undone immediately after. Fixed by adding exclude_unset to the handler's dump, with a guard that also pins the repo's half so the pair cannot drift. LIVE on the deployed image (2bb65b54f136): a summary-only update changed summary and PRESERVED name and visibility; a name-only update through the legacy tool changed name and preserved summary; a stale expected_version still returns the version conflict WITH the current row attached. The rest of the tool was already right: all four ops name their missing companion argument ('op=create requires code and name'), a duplicate code is refused by code, a foreign/missing arc_id gives the uniform deny, archive/restore round-trip with inverse undo hints, and visibility other than private is refused with the studio-UI guidance (#153 verified there is deliberately no agent path for that). Full unit suite 3620 passed.

composition_arc_template_update.note: PROVEN as the legacy twin of composition_arc_template_edit(op=update) and fixed by the SAME one-line change -- the unified tool delegates straight to this handler, so the not-null visibility failure was shared. Verified separately after the deploy: a name-only call through THIS tool changed name and preserved summary. See #155.

composition_arc_template_get.note: PROVEN by constructing its first invocation; no code change needed. An owned active template returns the full row; an owned ARCHIVED template is still readable, which it must be for composition_arc_template_restore to be usable at all; an unknown id gives the uniform deny. The read carries no embedding, source_ref or embedding_model even for the OWNER -- the projection is an allow-list rather than a model_dump, so the heavy/lineage columns cannot leak by being added to the table later. STATED LIMITATION rather than implied: the description says 'own or system', and this environment has ZERO system templates and zero public ones (0 of 53 rows), so the system branch could not be exercised. What was verified is the owned path and the deny; the system path is asserted by the same _VISIBLE_PREDICATE the list tools use (owner_user_id IS NULL OR visibility='public' OR owner_user_id=$1), but asserting is not measuring and this entry does not claim otherwise.

composition_arc_template_list.note: PROVEN with no code change, and it is the CONTRAST that makes #141 legible. This tool has a free-text `q` -- the same parameter that was a complete no-op on catalog_list_public_books -- and here it genuinely filters: q='zzznomatch' returns 0, q='Portable' returns exactly the matching template. Same idea, different service, done right; the catalogue's version was not a house pattern but a filter applied in the wrong service. Every other filter works too: scope=mine|system|all, status=draft|active|archived (an archived template IS listed under status=archived, so nothing is stranded), genre, and limit. limit=2 returns 2 with more=true; limit=999 returns 26 with more=false, matching the DB's own count of 26 active owned rows -- the denominator came from the database, not from the response. Each result carries a guidance line ('complete -- all N matching templates returned'), the same anti-loop affordance in the RESULT that the structure tools use. The stated guarantee 'embedding never projected' was MEASURED, not taken on trust: no embedding, embedding_model, embedded_summary_hash or source_ref appears in any row. OBSERVED, not filed: the schema describes limit as '1..100' in prose but declares no minimum/maximum, so limit=0 and limit=-1 are silently clamped to 1 rather than refused. Harmless -- more=true stays honest about the remainder -- and the same shape as #153's visibility enum, where prose narrows what the schema accepts. LIMITATION: scope=system returns 0 because this environment has no system templates at all (0 of 53 rows), so that scope is untested rather than verified empty.

composition_arc_template_restore.note: PROVEN with no code change; all four branches match the description exactly. Restoring an archived template of the caller's returns the full restored row; restoring it AGAIN (now active), restoring one that was never archived, and restoring an unknown id all give the uniform deny -- which is precisely what 'a foreign/system/not-archived id is not restorable' promises. The repo predicate is owner-scoped and status-scoped (WHERE (owner_user_id=$1 OR (book_shared AND book_id=$3)) AND id=$2 AND status='archived'), so the deny is a real no-op rather than a silent write. THE COST, recorded as DQ-19's second half rather than fixed: the deny for the caller's OWN ACTIVE template is false about a row they can fetch in full through composition_arc_template_get one call away. That is the same false-noun class the loop fixed seven times in book-service, and the same argument applies -- downstream of a passed ownership check there is no oracle left, so 'this template is not archived' would leak nothing. It stays recorded ONLY for consistency: DQ-19 declined to change archive's documented no-op-success on the loop's own authority, and fixing restore's message while leaving archive's would settle half a documented contract arbitrarily. Both halves want the same product decision and should get it together.

composition_arc_update.note: PROVEN with no code change -- and it is the CONTROL that explains why #155 broke. This is the same shape as composition_arc_template_update (a legacy update twin behind a unified op tool, partial semantics, OCC), and here partials work: title-only preserved summary and goal, status-only preserved title and summary, version bumped each time, and a stale expected_version returned applied_conflict rather than clobbering. THE DIFFERENCE IS WHERE 'partial' IS ENFORCED. StructureRepo.update skips Nones inside the REPO ('if value is None and field not in _NULLABLE_UPDATE_COLUMNS: continue'), so a handler that dumps every field as None cannot hurt it. ArcTemplateRepo.patch instead relied on the CALLER passing exclude_unset -- and the handler did not, which is exactly how every arc-template update came to fail on a NOT NULL visibility. Two repos, two strategies for the same word; only one is robust to caller sloppiness. That is the lesson worth carrying, not the one-line fix. expected_version is REQUIRED here rather than optional, so a blind clobber is impossible by construction. The undo_hint is the best the arc family has produced: it names composition_arc_update with the node_id, the PRIOR title, AND the post-write version, so replaying it actually restores the previous value instead of failing stale -- contrast #145, where hints minted through the unified tool point at de-advertised legacy tools, and #150's move, which honestly returns None because no single inverse exists.

composition_archive_derivative.note: PROVEN including the SAFETY guard, which is the one that mattered: archiving the CANONICAL Work is refused with 'NOT_A_DERIVATIVE -- archive applies only to a dị bản, not the canonical Work', and the canonical row was verified still active afterwards. A tool whose own name says 'derivative' but which would accept the canonical Work is a book-destroying typo away from disaster; it does not accept it. OCC is exemplary and does double duty: a stale expected_version returns {success:false, outcome:'applied_conflict', current_version:N} -- handing back the value the retry needs -- and re-archiving an already-archived derivative falls out of the SAME mechanism (the version moved to 2, so the old token is stale). No separate idempotency branch was needed, and none can drift out of sync with the first. PRECONDITION BUILT THROUGH THE REAL PATH, which is the method note worth keeping: no derivative was reachable, and composition_create_derivative is CONFIRM-GATED -- it returns a signed confirm_token and creates nothing. confirm_action is NOT an MCP tool (it belongs to the runtime's confirm flow), so the token was redeemed against composition-service's own POST /v1/composition/actions/confirm?token=... with a minted dev JWT. That produced a genuine derivative whose source_work_id points at the canonical Work -- a real branch, not a hand-written row. The pre-seeded fixture d0000000-... was NOT usable: it answered the uniform deny because its book is not one the caller holds a grant on, which is the gate working correctly rather than a bug. The derivative is left ARCHIVED on the throwaway book on purpose: composition_derivative_edit(op=restore) needs exactly that state to be proven when its turn comes.

composition_authoring_run_accept_unit.note: PROVEN against a real report_ready run (019f9f06...) on a book whose owner was read from the DB first, per DQ-17. Accepting a drafted unit returns {success:true, unit_index:8, status:'accepted'} and the row flips to accepted. Its refusals are the best-shaped in the composition service so far. Re-accepting says 'accept requires unit status=drafted, unit is accepted' -- it names the REQUIRED state and the ACTUAL one in the same sentence, which is precisely what #143 had to be taught after arc_assign_chapters reported a no-op as success. A bad unit_index says 'unit not found', correctly scoped to the unit rather than the book -- the false-noun class this loop fixed seven times elsewhere does not appear here. A run addressed through the WRONG book_id gives the uniform deny, which is right: the pair is the scope, and answering differently would make run ids probeable across books. Note the state change is left in place: unit 8 of that old test run stays accepted. Rejecting it would DISCARD its prose, which is a worse thing to do to real rows than leaving one unit accepted.

composition_authoring_run_close.note: PROVEN, and it was telling the caller that a SIBLING tool lies. Its description said the generic jobs_cancel 'does NOT work on a run (a run is not a background job; it silently no-ops)'. Measured with the `service` argument jobs_cancel actually requires: jobs_cancel(service='composition', job_id=<run_id>) returns {code:'NOT_FOUND', message:'not found or not accessible'} and the run stays report_ready. It refuses VISIBLY. The first half of the sentence is true and worth keeping -- jobs_cancel genuinely cannot stop a run -- but 'silently no-ops' is false, and the two call for OPPOSITE reactions: a silent no-op means 'this did nothing and told you nothing', an explicit deny means 'you addressed the wrong thing'. Teaching a model that a sibling lies makes it distrust a correct signal it will actually receive, the same misattributed-blame failure as #150. Corrected to name the answer jobs_cancel really gives, which also makes the warning verifiable rather than a claim. Deployed and read back off the live tools/list. The tool itself is sound: closing a report_ready run returns success and the row becomes closed; re-closing says 'close not allowed from status closed', naming the state; an unknown run_id gives the uniform deny. LIMITATION: no run was in the RUNNING state, so the 'pause a RUNNING run first' path is unverified rather than confirmed.

composition_authoring_run_gate.note: PROVEN through BOTH halves of its confirm-gated shape, which is what makes the conclusion worth anything: the propose returned a signed confirm_token with descriptor 'composition.authoring_run_gate' and changed NOTHING (the run was still draft afterwards), and the token was then redeemed against POST /v1/composition/actions/confirm to see what the description means by 'a failing check is reported at confirm time'. It reported: 'scope chapters not in this book: [019fb1cb-31d9-7525-8404-bb0c8bc657a2]' -- the exact offending id, not 'invalid scope'. That is the difference between an error a caller can act on and one it can only retry. And the run stayed DRAFT: a failed gate does not consume the book's one-active-run slot, so a bad scope cannot lock a book out of authoring. Fail-closed WITHOUT a side effect is the hard half and it holds. Both wrong-id cases (unknown run_id, and a real run addressed through another book) give the uniform deny -- correct, since book+run is the scope and answering differently would make run ids probeable across books. Incidental: the failure was genuine stale fixture data (a draft run whose scope names a chapter that is not in its book), so the check earned its keep on the first call.

composition_authoring_run_get.note: PROVEN with no code change, across the state boundary its description draws. A CLOSED run returns the run plus a populated per-unit report (unit_index entries); a DRAFT run returns the run with `units: null`; an unknown run_id gives the uniform deny. The null is the detail worth recording. `units: null` says 'no report exists for this status', where `units: []` would say 'the report exists and is empty' -- two different facts that a caller acts on differently, and the tool distinguishes them instead of flattening both into an empty list. That is the same class of honesty the loop has had to ADD elsewhere (#143's silent zero, #154's available:false-with-a-reason), here present already. Spend is visible on the run itself -- budget_usd 5.0000 against spent_usd 0.6000 -- so a caller can see how much of an autonomous run's budget is gone without a second call, which matters for the one tier where the tool spends the user's money.

composition_authoring_run_list.note: PROVEN with no code change; the listing is exact (10 runs returned against the DB's own count of 10 for that book -- the denominator came from the database, not the response), limit=3 returns 3, and an unknown book gives the uniform deny. THE FINDING IS A CONTRAST WORTH GENERALISING. This tool DECLARES its bound in the schema (limit: minimum 1, maximum 100), so limit=0 and limit=999 are rejected before the handler runs, with a message that names the field AND echoes the value: 'args.limit: Input should be greater than or equal to 1 (you sent ...)'. That is exactly the affordance #148 had to add BY HAND for malformed uuids -- name the field, show the caller its own value -- and here it costs nothing but declaring the constraint. Compare #158's composition_arc_template_list, whose description says '1..100' in PROSE while declaring no minimum/maximum: there limit=0 is silently clamped to 1 and the caller is never told. Same parameter, same service, two outcomes, and the whole difference is whether the bound is in the schema or only in a sentence. A constraint the schema knows about is enforced and explained for free; one that lives in prose is neither.

composition_authoring_run_manage.note: PROVEN with no code change. All five ops name their missing companion arguments exactly -- 'op=create requires plan_run_id, budget_usd, and pause_after_each_unit', 'op=start requires run_id', and so on -- so a flat-superset tool with a dozen optional fields never leaves the caller guessing which one an op wanted. DELEGATION PARITY PROVEN rather than assumed, the same check as #145: op=gate produced a confirm-token with descriptor 'composition.authoring_run_gate' -- byte-identical in kind to what the legacy composition_authoring_run_gate mints -- so the unified surface reaches the same handler and #164's confirm-time validation applies here too. WORTH RECORDING AS A SAFETY DESIGN: pause_after_each_unit is REQUIRED with no silent default, and the refusal names it. For a tool that starts an autonomous run spending the user's money, 'unattended' must be a thing the caller SAYS, never a thing it gets by omission. That is the opposite of the caller-supplied-value-defeats-a-default trap the loop has recorded elsewhere: here the absence of a default is the safety feature.

composition_authoring_run_pause.note: PROVEN on its refusal paths, with the happy path stated as unverified rather than implied. Pausing a DRAFT run answers 'pause requires status=running, run is draft' -- naming the required state AND the actual one, the same well-shaped refusal as accept_unit (#162). An unknown run_id gives the uniform deny. LIMITATION: no run was in the RUNNING state anywhere in the database, so running→paused could not be exercised. That is a gap in the evidence, not a defect, and it is recorded as a gap. The claim I COULD check without a running run is the security-relevant one, because it WIDENS permission: 'the book's OWNER-grant holder may pause ANY run on their book (not just their own)'. Verified at the source rather than assumed. _authoring_run_actor(..., allow_book_owner=True) returns immediately when the caller is the run's created_by; otherwise it requires GrantLevel.OWNER on the book, and a caller with neither gets the uniform deny. It also checks run.book_id != book_id first, so a run cannot be addressed through a book it does not belong to. And it returns run.created_by, so the pause is ATTRIBUTED to the run's owner rather than to the intervening admin -- the widening grants the ability to stop a collaborator's run without rewriting whose run it is.

composition_authoring_run_reject_unit.note: PROVEN including the destructive path, because the ordering promise is the whole tool and cannot be proven any other way. The description says it 'restores the chapter to its pre-run revision FIRST, then marks rejected (never rejected without the actual revert)'. MEASURED by hashing the chapter's draft body either side of the call: md5 ca2f0662... at 7389 chars BEFORE, md5 d7ca0192... at 64 chars AFTER -- the pre-run stub. The revert is real, not a status flip, and the response says reverted:true alongside status:'rejected'. A tool that marked rejected without reverting would leave the run report describing a chapter that still holds the run's prose, and that is exactly what this does not do. The cascade advisory is populated with REAL data rather than an empty courtesy field: cascade_warning.downstream_unit_indexes came back [1, 2] with a note explaining they were threaded on the rejected chapter's prose and are NOT auto-rejected (v1, advisory). Telling the caller what it did NOT do is the honest half of a destructive action. A bad unit_index says 'unit not found' -- scoped to the unit, not the book. RECOVERABILITY, checked rather than assumed before doing this to real rows: the unit still records post_revision_id, so the 7389 characters this reject discarded remain reachable through the chapter's revision history. Run on July fixture data (book 'Mị Đế', an earlier smoke), never on the dogfood book.

composition_authoring_run_resume.note: PROVEN through propose AND confirm, and the confirm half was telling the caller nothing. The propose mints a token even against a DRAFT run -- consistent with #164's gate, where the check lands at confirm time -- and the confirm correctly REFUSED, leaving the run draft. But it answered {'code': 'action_error'} with no reason at all, while its own sibling on the immediate path, composition_authoring_run_pause, says 'pause requires status=running, run is draft' for the same class of failure. The COST-GATED path, which is the only way to execute a W-tier action, told the caller less than the free one. The reason was caught and discarded: `except TransitionConflictError as exc:` raised a bare action_error and dropped exc. #164 already proved the mechanism supports detail ('scope chapters not in this book: [...]'), so nothing was missing but the argument. DATA and the reason the fix is NARROW: 65 raise sites in this router drop the reason and 3 keep it -- but most of the 65 MUST stay bare. LookupError (9) and (OwnershipError, InsufficientGrant) (8) are the anti-oracle denies, where a reason would confirm existence or access. TransitionConflictError (5) is the one class that cannot leak: a 409 means the caller already passed the book gate, and the only fact added is which state the run is in, which the direct-path tools already disclose. Fixed exactly those 5, with a test that also pins the anti-oracle catches STAYING bare so a later sweep does not 'finish the job' and turn a uniform deny into an oracle. LIVE on the deployed image: the same confirm now answers 'resume requires status=paused, run is draft' and the run is still draft. Full unit suite 3625 passed.

composition_authoring_run_revert_all.note: PROVEN end to end through propose AND confirm, on the same run #169 rejected a unit from. Every promise in the description was checked against the response rather than assumed. REVERSE ORDER, the load-bearing claim: reverted_unit_indexes came back [2, 1] -- NOT [1, 2]. Downstream first is what stops an earlier pre-run revision being restored over a later one, and the response proves the ordering rather than merely asserting it. Unit 0 was already rejected and was correctly not re-reverted. PARTIAL-FAILURE REPORTING is present and explicitly null on success: failed_unit_index: null, error: null. Fields that only appear when things go wrong are fields nobody can rely on; these are always there, so a caller can branch on them without guessing. FULL SUCCESS CLOSES THE RUN: run_status 'closed', closed: true, and the DB agrees -- all three units rejected, run closed. The propose mints a token even for a run in an illegal state (a closed one), consistent with #164's gate and #170's resume: the state check belongs at confirm time in this service, uniformly. After #170 that refusal now carries its reason, so the pattern is coherent across the whole confirm-gated family rather than coherent-but-silent. Run on July fixture data (book 'Mị Đế'); the discarded prose stays reachable through each unit's recorded post_revision_id, checked in #169 before any of this was done.

composition_authoring_run_review.note: PROVEN across all four ops, with delegation parity to the legacy tools confirmed by their messages coming through verbatim: op=pause gives 'pause requires status=running, run is closed' (#168), op=close gives 'close not allowed from status closed' (#163), and op=accept_unit on a closed run gives 'review requires run status in ('report_ready', 'failed', 'paused'), run is closed' -- which names the whole legal SET and the actual state, better than any single-state message could. Both unit ops name their missing companion ('op=accept_unit requires unit_index'). THE FINDING WAS IN THE SHARED KIT, not this tool. unit_index=-1 against the declared minimum:0 answered 'Input should be greater than or equal to 0 (you sent a int)'. 'a int' is a fact the caller already had; the one it needed was -1. loreweave_mcp's validation_directive rendered type(input).__name__ for every non-missing error, even though its own docstring says the clause is kept precisely because 'input really is the offending value'. It had the value and printed its type. Fixed in the kit with a _render_input helper: show repr(value), falling back to a type-and-length summary past 80 chars so a refusal never pastes a document back at the model. This is exactly the affordance #148 hand-rolled inside composition-service for uuids -- except here it lives in the one place every Python MCP service reads. Two existing kit tests pinned the old 'you sent a str' wording; they encoded the right INTENT (a non-missing error keeps a value clause) and were updated to assert the value, not deleted. The earlier missing-field guard still holds: a 'missing' error must never describe a value it did not receive, and a test pins that the sharper rendering did not resurrect it. LIVE on the deployed image: 'you sent -1'. Kit suite 1028 passed, composition 3625 passed. ROLLED OUT rather than left as a caveat: the kit is also read by jobs-, knowledge- and translation-service, so all three were rebuilt and force-recreated too, and the fix was re-measured on a DIFFERENT service to prove it travelled -- jobs_list with limit=-5 now answers 'you sent -5'. A shared-kit fix that only ships to the service you happened to be testing is three-quarters unshipped.

composition_canon_rule_create.note: PROVEN by constructing its first invocation; the tool writes what it is asked to write and the Undo hint is honest. Four rules created (world, entity, reveal_gate, and one with empty text) and all four cleaned up afterwards. OBSERVED, recorded rather than fixed: the tool accepts a rule with EMPTY text, a scope='entity' rule with no entity_id, and a reveal_gate with neither from_order nor until_order. An empty invariant cannot be satisfied or violated and still reaches the critic, which spends tokens on it; an entity-scoped rule that names no entity cannot bind to one. DATA is what keeps this a note: across the non-archived corpus there are ZERO empty-text rules and ZERO unbound entity rules -- the only instances that ever existed were the two I created to test the boundary. With no organic occurrence and no traffic, tightening this would be exactly the speculative 'better sentence' the runbook rules out, and it is left as a recorded observation like #153's enum and #158's prose-only bound. METHOD FAILURE WORTH MORE THAN THE OBSERVATION, and I nearly filed it as a defect: after deleting my four test rules I re-counted on the `active` column, saw them still true, and concluded that composition_canon_rule_delete AND composition_list_canon_rules were both broken -- 'refuses a rule that exists in the caller's own project'. They are not. canon_rule carries TWO flags, `active` and `is_archived`; delete sets is_archived, the list filters NOT is_archived, and re-deleting an already-archived rule correctly answers the uniform deny. Every one of those responses was right and my column was wrong. Reading the repository's actual predicate is what turned an invented cross-tool defect back into a clean cleanup -- the same shape as #149's denominator and #150's truncated-id ancestry.

composition_canon_rule_delete.note: PROVEN, and the result worth having is the CROSS-PROJECT guard, proven by attempting the thing it exists to stop rather than by reading its comment. The handler notes that canon.archive targets by id only, so a rule from another Work could be archived under THIS book's gate if the project scope were not checked first. Measured: passing another project's active rule_id together with my own project_id was DENIED, and that rule's is_archived was still false afterwards -- the deny is a real no-op, not a deny after the write. Checking the victim row is the difference between testing the message and testing the guard. The rest behaves: deleting an owned rule sets is_archived (leaving `active` alone -- the two flags are orthogonal, which is what misled me in #173), re-deleting an already-archived rule gives the uniform deny, and an unknown rule_id does too. Consistent with DQ-19's open question: the deny for the caller's OWN already-archived rule is uniform rather than 'already archived'. Same trade-off, same recorded question, not a new one.

composition_canon_rule_edit.note: PROVEN across all four ops with no code change, and it is the COUNTER-EXAMPLE to #155. That iteration found composition_arc_template_edit(op=update) completely broken -- every update wrote NULL over columns the caller never mentioned. This tool is the same shape and gets it right: op=update with only `text` changed the text and PRESERVED kind, scope and active. The difference is where partial-ness is enforced, exactly as #160 concluded -- CanonRulesRepo.update builds its SET list from the supplied patch rather than trusting the caller to have stripped its Nones. It also has the STRONGER contract of the two: expected_version is REQUIRED for op=update, not optional, and the refusal names all three missing pieces at once ('op=update requires project_id, rule_id, and expected_version'). A blind clobber is impossible by construction, where arc_template's optional version merely made one unlikely. A stale version returns applied_conflict WITH current_version, so the retry needs no extra read. delete→restore round-trips through is_archived and the text survives intact. All four ops name their missing companions precisely.

composition_canon_rule_restore.note: PROVEN as the exact inverse of #174, with the same guard tested the same way. Restoring an archived rule of the caller's own project brings it back (is_archived false, text intact). Restoring an ALREADY-live rule, an unknown rule_id, and -- the one that matters -- another project's archived rule under my own project_id all give the uniform deny, and the foreign rule was still archived afterwards. Checking the victim row is what separates a proven guard from a proven message. The pair delete↔restore is therefore symmetric in BOTH directions: each flips is_archived only for a rule that is genuinely in the gated Work's project, and each leaves everything else untouched. Note this is a flat rule list rather than a tree, so unlike the arc restore in #151 there is no ancestor chain to reconnect -- the asymmetry that mattered there simply does not arise here.

composition_canon_rule_update.note: PROVEN as the legacy twin of composition_canon_rule_edit(op=update) and, like #160's arc_update, it handles partials correctly: setting active=false alone changed only that, leaving text and kind intact. Reusing an already-consumed expected_version returns applied_conflict with current_version, so the version really is single-use rather than decorative. It also settles from the WRITE side the distinction that misled me in #173: `active` and `is_archived` are two different user actions, not two names for one. This tool toggles active (disable a rule while keeping it in the list); composition_canon_rule_delete sets is_archived (remove it from the list, reversibly). The row after active=false still had is_archived=false, so a disabled rule is NOT a deleted one -- and the critic's own read path (list_active: 'WHERE active AND NOT is_archived') needs both to be true, which is why each has its own tool.

composition_create_derivative.note: PROVEN through propose AND confirm (the full chain was first driven in #161), and it created a derivative at a NEGATIVE chapter index. branch_point is documented as a 0-based chapter index and nothing validated it: propose(branch_point=-5) minted a token, and confirming that token returned action_accepted with branch_point=-5 persisted on a real row. Deriving mints a fresh knowledge partition, is expensive, and is only ARCHIVABLE rather than undoable -- the tool's own description says so -- and a structurally impossible index survived both halves of a confirm-gated flow. DATA: 35 works carry a branch_point, every organic one is sane (0), and the single negative row was the one this iteration made. Latent, not active. Fixed by DECLARING the bound on the model (Field(ge=0)) rather than checking it in the handler, because #166 measured the difference in this same service: a bound the schema knows about is rejected before the handler runs and explained for free, while one living in a comment is neither. LIVE: -5 now answers 'Input should be greater than or equal to 0 (you sent -5)' -- the declared bound and #172's kit fix compounding -- and the control branch_point=0 still proposes, which is the off-by-one a gt=0 would have introduced (branching before chapter one is the most likely case of all). The other four guards were already right: deriving FROM a derivative is refused with 'CANNOT_DERIVE_FROM_DERIVATIVE -- branch from the canonical Work'; an empty name and a 250-character name both get 'name must be 1..200 characters'; and a bad taxonomy is a schema rejection listing the three valid values. All test derivatives were archived afterwards -- the throwaway book has none active.

composition_decompile_arcs.note: PROVEN end to end with no code change, and it is the GOOD version of the silent-clamp pattern this loop keeps finding. chapters_per_arc declares no minimum, so 0 and -1 are accepted and CLAMPED to 1 -- which on its own is the shape criticised in #158 and fixed in #178. Here it is defensible, and the reason is measurable rather than a matter of taste: the propose returns dry_run {chapters, would_create_arcs} AND a title that states the consequence, so chapters_per_arc=0 comes back as 'Decompile 2 chapter(s) into ~2 arc(s)' BEFORE anything is written. The clamp's effect is shown to the human who confirms it. A clamp whose consequence is displayed is a different thing from one that is not. THE DRY RUN IS ACCURATE, checked rather than trusted: it predicted would_create_arcs 1, the confirm created exactly 1 (book arcs 1 → 2) and assigned 2 chapters. A dry-run count that the write then contradicts would be worse than none, since it is the only thing the confirming human sees. IDEMPOTENCY, the other claim, also holds: re-running the whole propose→confirm cycle returned the SAME arc_id and left the count at 2 rather than minting a second arc over the same chapters. Cleaned up afterwards -- the book is back to its single pre-existing arc.

composition_derivative_edit.note: PROVEN across all three ops, and it gets RIGHT the exact distinction #155 got wrong. op=update_spec must tell 'field omitted' (leave it alone) apart from 'field explicitly null' (clear it) -- its description promises both -- and both were measured: setting pov_anchor + canon_rule, then updating taxonomy ALONE left pov_anchor and canon_rule intact, then passing pov_anchor:null cleared that field while canon_rule survived. That is the hard case with pydantic, it is precisely what exclude_unset exists for, and it is what composition_arc_template_edit collapsed into 'everything is None' before #155. THE SAFETY GUARDS hold on both destructive ops: op=archive and op=restore against the CANONICAL Work are each refused with 'NOT_A_DERIVATIVE -- <op> applies only to a dị bản, not the canonical Work', naming the op rather than one generic sentence. Restoring the derivative #161 deliberately left archived brought it back to active. SMALL AFFORDANCE NOTE: pov_anchor is declared as a plain string but must be an entity UUID. Sending a name answered 'pov_anchor must be a UUID -- received Nguyet' -- #148's helper doing its job, so the caller self-corrects in one round trip rather than guessing. The derivative was re-archived afterwards; the throwaway book has no active derivative.

composition_diagnostics.note: PROVEN with no code change, and its headline claim -- 'counts are exact; rows are capped' -- was tested rather than believed. At limit=25 it returned 2 items with counts {conformance_never_run: 1, unplanned_chapter: 1}, total 2, refs_capped false. At limit=1 it returned ONE item row while counts and total STAYED 2 and refs_capped flipped to true. So the cap never distorts the numbers and the truncation is DECLARED -- the exact opposite of the silent-truncation failure where a capped list reads as the complete set. conformance_never_run:1 was reproduced against the database exactly. unplanned_chapter I could NOT independently reproduce, and that is a note about my query, not the tool: I counted outline nodes with no structure_node_id (2) while the diagnostic comes from compute_coverage, a planned-vs-written diff over BOOK chapters. Different populations, so the numbers were never comparable -- the same 'check the definition before calling it a mismatch' lesson as #149 and #173. WORTH RECORDING: that coverage call has a `degraded` branch, and when it trips the tool appends 'the planned-vs-written diff degraded -- unplanned chapters UNKNOWN' instead of reporting zero. A problems panel that silently shows no problems when it could not look is the worst possible failure for a health check, and this one distinguishes 'none' from 'could not tell'.

composition_divergence_spec_update.note: PROVEN as the legacy twin of composition_derivative_edit(op=update_spec) (#180) and it behaves identically, which is what delegation parity is supposed to look like. The canonical Work is refused with 'NOT_A_DERIVATIVE -- the spec exists only on a dị bản', and passing canon_rule ALONE left taxonomy and pov_anchor untouched. TWO SEMANTICS WORTH STATING because a caller could reasonably assume otherwise. First, canon_rule is REPLACED wholesale, not appended: [r1, r2] became [only-this]. That is consistent with 'only the fields you pass change' -- the field changed, in full -- but an agent asked to 'add a rule' must read the current list and send the union, or it will silently drop the others. Second, the spec of an ARCHIVED derivative is still editable. Nothing forbids it and it is arguably right (fix the spec, then restore), but it does mean 'archived' constrains the Work's lifecycle rather than freezing its spec.

composition_entity_override_add.note: PROVEN by constructing its first invocation. The two guards it advertises both hold: the canonical Work is refused with 'NOT_A_DERIVATIVE -- overrides exist only on a dị bản', and a second override for the same entity is refused with 'OVERRIDE_EXISTS -- an override for this entity already exists; update it instead' -- which names the remedy rather than just the collision, so a caller that meant to change an existing override knows where to go. OBSERVED, recorded rather than fixed, both with the same denominator argument as #173: an override with EMPTY overridden_fields is accepted (an override that overrides nothing), and target_entity_id is not checked for existence -- a completely fabricated UUID was accepted and stored. The second is defensible in a way the first is not: entities live in glossary-service, so validating would be a cross-service round trip on every add. DATA: the entire non-archived override corpus was 2 rows, BOTH created by this iteration, so the organic population of either anomaly is ZERO. With no measured occurrence and no traffic, tightening either would be the speculative change the runbook rules out. Both test rows were deleted afterwards; the table is back to empty.

composition_entity_override_delete.note: PROVEN. Deleting an owned override soft-archives it (is_archived true) and returns an undo_hint naming composition_entity_override_add with the arguments to recreate it -- a genuinely replayable inverse, unlike the arc family's hints that point at de-advertised legacy tools (#145). Re-deleting and an unknown override_id both give the uniform deny. ASYMMETRY WORTH RECORDING, not filed as a defect: passing the CANONICAL Work's project_id gives the uniform deny here, while its sibling composition_entity_override_add answers 'NOT_A_DERIVATIVE -- overrides exist only on a dị bản'. The difference is structural rather than a policy inconsistency: delete has an override_id to look up and genuinely does not find one under the canonical project, so 'not found' is literally true. But the consequence for a caller who mistyped the project_id is that add tells it the real problem while delete sends it hunting for a bad override_id. The better message demonstrably exists in the same family and would leak nothing (the caller supplied the canonical id itself), so this is a cheap consistency win whenever the family is next touched -- left recorded rather than changed because the tool has zero traffic and no measured failure, the same bar applied in #153, #158 and #183.

composition_entity_override_edit.note: PROVEN across all four ops, and the claim worth testing was the CONFLICT one: op=restore 'FAILS if a newer override for that same entity now exists, which is honest rather than clobbering the newer one'. Constructed exactly that race -- add, delete, add a NEW override for the same entity, then restore the OLD one -- and it refused, leaving the old one archived and the new one untouched. This is the one-override-per-entity uniqueness resolved by REFUSAL rather than by a silent overwrite, which is the failure mode this repo has hit before (a remediation that writes a shared key without merging first). Restoring by clobbering would have destroyed a deliberate newer decision to recover an older discarded one -- strictly the wrong direction. The refusal also names BOTH possible causes ('it was never deleted, or a newer override for that entity...'), because from the caller's side those are indistinguishable and picking one would be a guess. All four ops name their missing companions precisely. Test rows cleaned up; the override table is empty again.

composition_entity_override_restore.note: PROVEN on the HAPPY path that #185's conflict test could not reach: with no rival override, restore returns {restored: true}, is_archived flips to false, AND overridden_fields survives intact ({'name': 'NEWER'}). That last part is the one worth checking -- a restore that recovered the row but not its content would look identical in the response and be useless in effect. Re-restoring an already-live override and an unknown override_id both give the same combined refusal ('it was never deleted, or a newer override for that entity...'). For the unknown id that sentence is technically loose -- the id does not exist at all, which is a third case -- but the looseness is deliberate: naming which of the three applies would confirm whether an override_id exists. The anti-oracle posture costs a little precision here and buys the same protection the rest of this service applies.

composition_entity_override_update.note: PROVEN, and it is REPLACE rather than merge -- measured: {name:A, role:villain} updated with {name:B} became {name:B}, dropping role. The description says so plainly ('the whole overridden_fields JSON is replaced -- the override IS the delta') and the parenthetical is the justification, not decoration: if updating merged, there would be no way to REMOVE a field from the delta, so a role override applied once could never be taken back. This completes a consistent picture across the service that is worth stating as a rule: SCALAR fields are partial (omit one and it is unchanged -- canon_rule_update #177, arc_update #160, derivative update_spec #180), while COLLECTION and delta fields are replaced wholesale (canon_rule[] in #182, overridden_fields here). Every tool that does the latter says so in its description. An agent asked to 'also override role' must therefore read the current fields and send the union -- the same trap #182 records for canon_rule.

composition_find_references.note: PROVEN against a real referenced entity rather than an unused one -- the first candidate returned all zeros, which would have proven nothing about the counting. Found an entity actually present in scenes and verified: scene_present count=2, matching the database's own count of 2 for that (book, entity). At limit=1 the rows dropped to 1 while the count STAYED 2 and has_more flipped to true. So 'exact counts plus a capped sample' holds PER SOURCE, with the truncation declared per source rather than once for the whole response -- a caller can tell which of the eight sources it has only partially seen. Same discipline as #181's diagnostics. An unknown source name is rejected at the schema, listing all eight valid values and echoing what was sent. SCOPE HONESTY worth noting: the description states outright that this covers the SPEC layer only and names the two tools for the other layers (glossary_get_entity for prose links, kg_entity_edge_timeline for the graph), saying explicitly 'this tool does not federate to them'. A find-references that silently covered one third of the places an entity can appear would be actively misleading; naming its own boundary and the complements is what makes a zero here safe to act on.

composition_generate.note: PROVEN END TO END, including the paid half, at ZERO cash cost -- the propose was driven with model_source=user_model against a LOCAL lm_studio model (nvidia/nemotron-3-nano) found via settings_list_models, rather than the platform cloud model. Local-first is the house rule and here it is also what makes a W-tier tool provable without spending the user's money. The cost gate holds: the propose returns descriptor composition.generate, a title naming the model, and an explicit `requires` field ('human confirmation via the review surface -- this spends LLM tokens; nothing is generated until...'), and it wrote NOTHING (0 rows in generation_job). Confirming created job 019ff100-8e9d... status pending, which reached status=completed with a 4902-character result. 'EXACTLY ONE of outline_node_id / chapter_id' is enforced in BOTH directions -- neither id and both ids give the same message, which also explains what each argument means ('a scene' / 'a whole chapter'), so a caller that supplied the wrong one learns which it wanted. A bad model_source is a schema rejection listing both valid values and echoing what was sent. HONEST DEGRADATION worth recording: the result pack carries warnings ['grounding_unavailable: no knowledge-graph data for this scene/project (C3a)']. The engine ran and produced prose while SAYING it had no canon to ground against, rather than presenting ungrounded output as grounded -- the distinction that matters most for a tool whose entire selling point is canon-grounded drafting.

composition_get_derivative_context.note: PROVEN. The derivative returns its full durable spec -- is_derivative true, name, source_work_id AND source_project_id, taxonomy, branch_point, pov_anchor, canon_rules -- and the canon_rules came back as ['only-this'], which independently confirms #182's wholesale-replacement finding persisted rather than merged. THE CANONICAL WORK GETS A TRUTHFUL ANSWER, not an error: {is_derivative: false}. That is the right shape for a READ and a deliberate contrast with its write-side siblings (entity_override_add, derivative_edit, archive_derivative), which all refuse the canonical Work with NOT_A_DERIVATIVE. Asking 'is this a derivative?' is a legitimate question with a legitimate 'no'; asking to ARCHIVE a derivative that is actually the canonical Work is a mistake. Same fact, two correct responses, because the questions differ -- and it means a caller can CHECK before attempting a write instead of learning by refusal. The description also draws the distinction that makes the tool worth having: this is the persisted substrate the packer applies at retrieval, NOT the derive-time cache -- so it answers what will actually be applied, which is the only version worth reading.

composition_get_generation_job.note: PROVEN against the REAL job #189 created rather than a synthetic id -- the two iterations are the two halves of one flow, and polling a job you did not produce proves much less. It returns everything the description promises: status completed, the generated `result` (the pack, including its grounding warnings), model_ref, and cost_usd 0.0000 -- which independently confirms that routing #189's W-tier proof through a local lm_studio model cost nothing, rather than my having assumed it. SCOPING is the pair, proven by attempting the miss: an unknown job_id AND the real job addressed under a DIFFERENT project_id both give the uniform deny. So job ids are not probeable across projects, and a caller holding a job id from elsewhere learns nothing by pointing it at a project it can read. The result also carries a per-stage status (skipped_no_cast) alongside the job-level one, so 'the job completed' and 'every stage ran' stay separable -- a job that completed with stages skipped is exactly the case a single status field would hide.

composition_get_prose.note: PROVEN, and it CROSS-CONFIRMS #189: the chapter body now opens 'The incense smoke curled in the air, thick and grey...' -- prose the cowrite engine generated two iterations ago. The generate→job→prose chain is therefore proven end to end across three tools, each verified against the artefact the previous one produced rather than against a fixture. detail=summary does exactly what it claims: 1069 bytes with no `body` versus 3107 with it, and CRUCIALLY the same draft_version (4) in both. That is the whole point of the mode -- its stated use is 'when you only need the version to prep a write', so a summary that dropped the concurrency token would be pure cost with no benefit. Checking that the token survives the projection is the only thing that makes the mode worth having. A chapter addressed under the wrong project_id gives the uniform deny, so the pair is the scope here as elsewhere in this service.

composition_glossary_build.note: PROVEN on the plan half of its six-op pipeline, driven with a LOCAL lm_studio model so a paid tool cost nothing (the #189 method). op=start returned run_id, status plan_ready and a worklist (Lan, character, standard depth) and BUILT NOTHING -- op=status then reported items: [] against the same run, which is the check that matters: the description insists 'always show the user the worklist before approving it', and a start that quietly began building would make that instruction unfollowable. The plan/build separation is real, not just described. op=cancel moved it to cancelled, and op=approve_plan afterwards was refused with 'BAD_STATE: run is not in plan_ready' -- naming the required state, so a caller cannot resurrect a cancelled run by retrying. All six ops name their missing argument. ONE SMALL DIFFERENCE from its siblings, worth recording: op=start reports missing arguments SEQUENTIALLY -- with both absent it named only model_ref, and source_text only after model_ref was supplied. arc_edit and run_manage name all missing companions at once ('requires plan_run_id, budget_usd, and pause_after_each_unit'), which costs one round trip instead of two. NOT PROVEN and stated as such: approve_plan → build → project_kg → approve_edges were not run. Building would create real glossary drafts and graph edges on the book, and the plan gate is the half that carries the safety claim.

composition_library_translate.note: PROVEN end to end through propose → confirm → background job → persisted translation, on a LOCAL model so a paid tool cost nothing. Title rendered the target language in its own script ('Translate 1 motif(s) to Tiếng Việt'), the job reached completed with per-item status 'translated', and one motif_translation row exists. THE COST CLAIM IS REAL, and it is the one worth measuring on a paid tool: 'an existing, still-current translation is skipped rather than re-charged unless force=true'. Re-running the identical request produced per-item status 'already_translated' and the translation row count stayed at 1 -- no duplicate row, no second charge. A skip that silently re-translated would be indistinguishable in the response and would bill the user twice. THE PLATFORM GUARD holds and teaches: a built-in (owner_user_id NULL) motif is refused with 'none of those motifs are yours to translate -- the built-in library already ships in every supported language...', so the caller learns why rather than just that it failed. Empty ids is refused; a bad target_language is a schema rejection listing all 17 codes. AFFORDANCE WORTH COPYING: the confirm response carries "poll": "composition_get_mine_job" -- the async handoff NAMES the tool that continues the flow instead of leaving an agent to infer it from the description.

composition_list_derivatives.note: PROVEN for what it does: passing ANY Work's project_id from the book returns the canonical Work with is_canonical, name, branch_point, status and version -- and passing an ARCHIVED derivative's own project_id resolves to the same book rather than erroring, which is the 'any Work's project_id' promise working. THE FINDING, recorded as DQ-20: it lists ACTIVE works only, with no include_archived or status parameter, so the book's two archived derivatives are invisible -- and this is NOT agent-only. The REST route list_book_derivatives is documented as the twin of this tool and the DivergenceManagerView's read side, and both call works.resolve_by_book, whose query filters status='active'. The product's own divergence manager is equally blind. The cause is a shared primitive with two callers wanting opposite things: resolve_by_book is the work-RESOLUTION chokepoint, where excluding an archived Work is CORRECT, and it is being reused as a listing read, where it is exactly wrong. Each caller's fix is the other's defect.
