The consequence is concrete -- derivative_edit op=restore works (#180) but its input is discoverable only if the caller kept the id -- and the sibling precedent is right there (arc_list's include_archived, arc_template_list's status). Recorded rather than edited because choosing wrong turns a listing convenience into a resolution bug.

composition_motif_adopt.note: PROVEN through propose and confirm. A system motif proposes a clone; an unknown motif_id gives the uniform deny; target='book' without book_id is refused with 'book_id is required when target=book', naming the conditional dependency rather than failing generically. Confirming produced a real clone in my library. A HYPOTHESIS I TESTED AND DROPPED, which is the part worth recording. Adopting my OWN motif is accepted and clones it, giving two motifs with code 'duel' in one library. Since #146 established that arc-template placements resolve motifs BY CODE, I expected that to make resolution ambiguous -- a real defect chain. It does not. MotifRepo.get_by_codes orders '(owner_user_id = $1) DESC NULLS LAST, owner_user_id NULLS FIRST, version DESC', so among a caller's own same-code motifs the highest version wins DETERMINISTICALLY. And duplicates are not exotic: 3 duplicate (owner, code) pairs already exist organically, independent of anything this iteration did. The system tolerates duplicate codes by design with an explicit precedence rule, so self-adopt is a 'duplicate this motif' operation rather than a corruption. Checking the ORDER BY before writing the finding is what kept this from being a fabricated defect -- the same discipline as #149, #173 and #181. The clone was archived afterwards; one active 'duel' remains.

composition_motif_archive.note: PROVEN, and the tenancy guard was tested on the VICTIM row rather than on the message: archiving a SYSTEM motif (owner_user_id NULL) gives the uniform deny AND that motif's status was still 'active' afterwards. A read-only-to-you row that answers 'not accessible' while quietly flipping would look identical in the response, so checking the row is the only version of this test that means anything -- the same method as #174's cross-project canon rule. An unknown motif_id gives the uniform deny. Archiving an owned motif returns archived:true with an undo_hint, and re-archiving is idempotent rather than an error -- the same shape as book_structure_part_archive (#138), arc_delete (#144) and arc_restore (#151), so the whole archive family in this repo agrees that the state asked for being the state that holds is a success. The motif was restored afterwards, because #146's arc template resolves its placements against this motif BY CODE and leaving it archived would have silently changed what a later apply resolves.

composition_motif_bind.note: PROVEN, and the safety claim -- 'Re-binding over a prior motif ARCHIVES (never deletes) the affected scenes' -- was measured by counting rows on both sides rather than trusting the word. Scene rows under the chapter went 2 live/0 archived/2 TOTAL, then after binding 'duel' 2 live/2 archived/4 total, then after re-binding 'ambush' 2 live/4 archived/6 total. The live count stays at the new motif's beat count while the TOTAL only ever grows -- which is exactly what 'never deletes' has to look like in the data, and is a stronger check than any response field because a delete would still leave live=2. The response also returns archived_scene_ids explicitly, so the caller knows WHICH scenes were retired by its swap rather than having to diff the outline itself. A destructive-looking operation that names what it displaced is the difference between reversible and merely recoverable-in-principle. State left behind, deliberately: the chapter is now bound to 'ambush' with 4 archived scenes underneath it on the throwaway book. That is a coherent end state for the tool (every re-bind leaves its predecessors archived), not debris to clean -- un-archiving them would produce a chapter with three motifs' scenes live at once, which is precisely what the archiving prevents.

composition_motif_bind_edit.note: PROVEN across both ops AND both UNBIND MODES, which is the whole point of this tool over the legacy pair. The description distinguishes 'pass the bind's undo_token to do the EXACT inverse' from 'omit to CLEAR the chapter's motif', and they behave differently in exactly the way that matters: omitting it returned {cleared: true} and took live scenes 2 → 0, while passing it returned {undone: true, restored_scene_ids: [...]} with live staying at 2 and the TOTAL unchanged at 12. The undo UN-ARCHIVED the previous binding's scenes rather than clearing the chapter -- a real inverse, not a differently-worded delete. The two response shapes differ (`cleared` vs `undone`/`restored_scene_ids`), so a caller can tell which of the two it got without inspecting the outline. Total row count never moved during the undo, consistent with #198: this family only ever flips archive flags. ONE SCHEMA NOTE, learned the hard way: undo_token is an OBJECT ({chapter_node_id, archived_scene_ids, new_scene_ids}), not an opaque string. I passed a string first and got 'args.undo_token: Input should be a valid dictionary (you sent ...)' -- #172's kit fix naming the field, the expected type AND the value, which is what made the mistake self-correcting in one round trip.

composition_motif_create.note: PROVEN. A minimal create works; target='book_shared' without book_id is refused naming the conditional dependency; bad `kind` and `visibility` are schema rejections listing the valid values and echoing what was sent; a duplicate code returns applied_conflict with 'a motif with this code already exists in your library'. THIS CORRECTS AND COMPLETES #196. There I found adopt creating a second 'duel' motif and reasoned it was harmless because code resolution is deterministic. The real explanation is sharper: uniqueness is enforced by FOUR PARTIAL indexes, one per tier -- uq_motif_user (owner, code) WHERE book_id IS NULL; uq_motif_user_book (owner, book_id, code); uq_motif_book_shared (book_id, code); uq_motif_system (code) WHERE owner IS NULL. The original 'duel' is book_shared, the adopted clone is user-tier, so they sit under DIFFERENT indexes and violate nothing. Same code at two tiers is intended, not tolerated. A REAL FINDING fell out of testing that: creating 'duel' at the user tier is now REFUSED, because #196's clone -- which I ARCHIVED -- still occupies uq_motif_user. The partial indexes do not exclude archived rows, so an archived motif keeps reserving its code. That is defensible (restoring it would otherwise collide) but the MESSAGE is not: 'a motif with this code already exists in your library' names a row the caller can no longer see in their library, which is the same shape as DQ-20's invisible-but-blocking archived derivative. Saying 'it may be archived -- restore it or choose another code' would cost nothing and name the way out. Recorded rather than reworded: zero traffic, and the runbook rules out prose changes without measured failure.

composition_motif_edit.note: PROVEN across all four ops. Each names its missing companions ('op=patch requires motif_id and expected_version'). op=patch is genuinely PARTIAL -- patching `name` alone left kind and summary intact -- which puts it with canon_rule_edit (#175) and arc_update (#160) on the correct side of the divide #155 exposed, where composition_arc_template_edit wrote NULL over every unmentioned column. A stale expected_version returns applied_conflict with current_version. archive→restore→archive round-trips with undo hints on each step. Consistent with #187's rule for this service: SCALAR fields are partial, and the COLLECTION fields this tool also accepts (roles, beats, effects) are the replace-wholesale kind -- worth knowing before an agent 'adds a beat' and silently drops the rest, the same trap recorded for canon_rule[] (#182) and overridden_fields (#187).

composition_motif_get.note: PROVEN, and the ownership PROJECTION was proven by DIFFING THE FIELD SETS rather than by reading the allow-list constant. Reading my own motif returns owner_user_id, source_ref, examples, code and status; reading a SYSTEM motif I do not own returns only code and status -- owner_user_id, source_ref and examples are absent, and no embedding appears either way. That matches the _MOTIF_PUBLIC_FIELDS allow-list's stated intent ('NEVER the embedding vector, the raw source_ref lineage, the copied examples[], or owner_user_id') and, unlike quoting the constant, it proves the allow-list is actually APPLIED on this path. An allow-list defined and not wired is the exact failure #146 found elsewhere in this service. My own ARCHIVED motif is still readable in full, which it must be for op=restore to be usable -- the same property #157 established for arc templates. An unknown motif_id gives the uniform deny.

composition_motif_link_create.note: PROVEN, with all four promised refusals exercised. A self-link is refused; a valid duel→ambush `precedes` edge is created; repeating it returns applied_conflict 'that edge already exists'; the reverse edge ambush→duel is refused as a CYCLE (a real 2-cycle, constructed rather than assumed); and an endpoint I do not own (a system motif) gives the uniform deny, so the system graph is genuinely read-only to a user. The self-link and cycle share one message that ENUMERATES its causes -- 'invalid edge (self-link, cycle, or cross-tier)'. That is the acceptable version of the shape #150 had to fix on composition_arc_move: there the message actively MISATTRIBUTED, reporting a cycle as a depth violation and sending the caller to fix the wrong thing. Listing three possibilities without claiming the wrong one is different in kind -- and here the caller holds both ids, so a self-link is self-evident from its own arguments and a cycle is discoverable with composition_motif_link_list.

composition_motif_link_delete.note: PROVEN. Deleting an owned edge returns {deleted: true} and the row is GONE -- count 0, a HARD delete, unlike every other delete in this service (motifs, canon rules, entity overrides, arcs, derivatives all soft-archive). That is not an inconsistency: motif_link has no lifecycle column at all (id, from_motif_id, to_motif_id, ord, created_at, kind), so the table was designed for hard deletes. An edge carries no authored content -- it is three ids and an ordinal -- so there is nothing to preserve for recovery the way a motif's beats or a chapter's prose must be. Re-deleting and an unknown link_id both give the uniform deny. OBSERVED: undo_hint is null. Honest for a hard delete in the sense that nothing can be un-deleted -- but a REPLAYABLE hint was available here, since composition_motif_link_create takes exactly the four values this row held, which is precisely what #184's entity_override_delete does (its hint names override_add with the arguments to recreate it). The one thing a replay would lose is the row id, which nothing references. Recorded, not filed: #122 established that undo_hint is explicitly non-contractual with no consumer in the tree.

composition_motif_link_edit.note: PROVEN on both ops with delegation parity confirmed rather than assumed: op=create refused a real 2-cycle (duel composed_of ambush, then ambush composed_of duel) with the message byte-identical to #203's legacy composition_motif_link_create, and op=delete removed the edge through the same path. Both ops name their missing companions ('op=create requires from_motif_id, to_motif_id, and kind'). Worth noting the cycle guard applies per KIND: #203 proved it on `precedes`, this proved it on `composed_of`, which are the two the description says it guards -- variant_of is deliberately excluded, and that asymmetry is stated rather than silent ('a cycle (on composed_of/precedes) is refused'). A variant-of cycle is meaningful (two motifs can each be a variant of the other) where a composition or succession cycle is not.

composition_motif_link_list.note: PROVEN against two real edges built for the test (duel precedes ambush, duel variant_of meet), so every filter was checked against a known expected answer rather than an empty graph. direction='both' and 'out' return both edges; 'in' on duel returns nothing (nothing points at it); and -- the decisive one -- 'in' on AMBUSH returns the precedes edge, i.e. the SAME row seen from the other endpoint. That proves direction genuinely inverts the traversal rather than being a label on a fixed result set. kinds=['precedes'] filters to one. Each row carries the neighbor's id, code AND name inline, which is what makes the description's 'walk the graph by following a neighbor id into another list call' actually workable: a traversal needs no second lookup per hop just to know what it reached. Both test edges were deleted afterwards.
